ocar.opportunity: Connectomics depends on segmenting neurons, synapses, and organelles such as mitochondria from nanometer-scale volumetric microscopy before structural or functional analysis can proceed. Deep learning is now the default for both semantic and instance segmentation on biomedical volumes.
ocar.challenge: Open-source segmentation packages are typically built for standard benchmarks, so adapting them to connectomics data of different scales and formats takes substantial work on hardware and preprocessing. Specialized architectures and learning targets are cumbersome to implement, and expensive expert labels sit beside large unlabeled volumes that most packages do not exploit.
ocar.action: Lin, Wei, Lichtman, and Pfister present PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC), an open-source PyTorch framework for 2D and 3D semantic and instance segmentation. Configuration options, without new code, enable multi-task and semi-supervised learning and retargeting to other tissues and imaging modalities.
ocar.resolution: On the CREMI challenge, PyTC reports the best synaptic-cleft segmentation, outperforming the previous best result by a relative 6.1%, with competitive performance on mitochondria and neuronal nuclei. Code and tutorials are released at connectomics.readthedocs.io.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract does not specify a follow-on reconstruction campaign; the natural next uses are applying the same configuration-driven pipeline to additional organelles, volumes, and imaging modalities.

summaries.beginner: Computers must paint every pixel of a brain microscope volume before anyone can follow the wiring. This paper shares an open toolbox, PyTorch Connectomics, that trains those painting models on big three-dimensional images without rewriting code for each new dataset.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv preprint (2021), Lin, Wei, Lichtman, and Pfister introduce PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC) for semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy. The toolbox is aimed at connectomics-scale neuron, synapse, and organelle segmentation and supports multi-task and semi-supervised training so scarce expert labels can be combined with unlabeled data. On CREMI synaptic-cleft segmentation it reports a relative 6.1% improvement over the previous best result, with competitive mitochondria and neuronal-nuclei scores.
summaries.advanced: The 6.1% figure is a relative CREMI synaptic-cleft gain, not a neuron-instance score; mitochondria and nuclei results are described only as competitive. The selected PDF extract is dominated by front matter and references, so claims about production-scale reconstructions or other tasks rest on the abstract and introduction rather than a full results section. Generalization beyond the reported benchmarks is asserted via configuration, not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Computers must paint every pixel of a brain microscope volume before anyone can follow the wiring. This paper shares an open toolbox, PyTorch Connectomics, that trains those painting models on big three-dimensional images without rewriting code for each new dataset.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical inhibitory neurons come in many physiological, morphological, molecular, and connectivity flavors. Mapping how a defined interneuron class innervates identified targets at synaptic resolution is a route to linking cell type, structure, and function.
ocar.challenge: Average connectivity of several interneuron classes is known, but the synaptic-resolution distribution of a distinct inhibitory type, how that distribution relates to target-cell properties, and how it affects function remain poorly understood.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell and colleagues used dense electron microscopy in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex plus cell-type-specific calcium imaging in awake animals. They mapped complete chandelier-cell input onto 153 pyramidal neurons and simulated the observed axo-axonic pattern.
ocar.resolution: Chandelier synapse number is highly variable across pyramids, correlates with target structural features, and varies more than perisomatic inhibition; simple perisomatic features already accounted for approximately half the variance in chandelier synapse count. Simulations indicate the pattern is especially effective when excitation and inhibition are co-active. In vivo, chandelier cells fire in highly correlated bouts that track pupil dilation, a proxy for arousal.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag a larger volume (Bae et al., 2021) to reduce truncation and add morphology, activity, and excitatory-network covariates. Whether P36 connectivity is adult-mature, and whether remaining filopodia mark plasticity or incomplete maturation, needs older-animal datasets.

summaries.beginner: Some inhibitory cells grab the axon of a neighbor right where it starts its output spike. This paper maps those chandelier connections onto many visual-cortex pyramids in a mouse and shows the cells fire together when the animal is aroused.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Schneider-Mizell, da Costa, and colleagues reconstructed chandelier input onto 153 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse visual cortex from dense electron microscopy and imaged chandelier activity in awake mice. Synapse counts vary widely, more than perisomatic inhibition, and correlate with target structure; perisomatic features explained about half of chandelier-count variance. Biophysical simulations suggest axo-axonic inhibition is especially effective when excitation and inhibition coincide. Population calcium signals are highly correlated and track pupil dilation.
summaries.advanced: The EM volume is from postnatal day 36, just after the critical period; adulthood is usually taken as P56, and occasional chandelier filopodia leave open whether the map is fully mature. Functional imaging and EM are not from the same cells. Volume truncation and missing whole-cell morphology are explicit limits; about half the chandelier-count variance remains unexplained by the simple features used here.

plain_language_summary: Some inhibitory cells grab the axon of a neighbor right where it starts its output spike. This paper maps those chandelier connections onto many visual-cortex pyramids in a mouse and shows the cells fire together when the animal is aroused.

ocar.opportunity: The circuits that generate animal behavior remain largely unknown. A dense map of neurons and chemical synapses in a complex brain would let many circuit questions become lookups rather than months of experiment.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing a large fraction of a sophisticated brain requires better sample preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse detection, and proofreading, plus a way to define cell types and share an evolving dataset.
ocar.action: Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and a large Janelia–Google collaboration present the adult Drosophila central-brain (hemibrain) connectome. They summarize pipeline improvements, define cell types, refine compartments, and release public circuits of neurons and chemical synapses.
ocar.resolution: The resource provides a census of central-brain neurons and types, an atlas of regions, and a connectivity graph. Analyses include connection-strength distributions unlike those reported in mammals, motifs such as cliques, electrical effects of compartmentalization, and evidence that packing density shaped the wiring. Partner lookup that once took months is reduced to a web query.
ocar.future_work: Not all hemibrain regions were read to the highest accuracy; central complex and mushroom body were prioritized. Updates to remaining regions, distributed systems such as clock and modulatory neurons, graph–function links, and comparison of the two sexes are flagged as underway or obvious next steps.

summaries.beginner: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and colleagues report the hemibrain connectome of the adult Drosophila central brain. They improve preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse finding, and proofreading, then define cell types and computational compartments and release neuron-and-chemical-synapse circuits. Analyses cover strength distributions, motifs, compartmental electrical effects, and packing-density constraints. The data are public so upstream and downstream partners can be queried rather than rediscovered experimentally.
summaries.advanced: The map is chemical synapses in a large fraction of the central brain of one animal, not a whole-animal nervous system and not gap junctions. Completeness varies by region; central complex and mushroom body were prioritized. The authors themselves note that synaptic richness far exceeds identified behaviors, so many pathways remain uninterpreted. Sex differences are acknowledged as unfinished.

plain_language_summary: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.

ocar.opportunity: Complete circuits have been reconstructed in small animals with hundreds of neurons, and selected circuits in larger ones. A dense map of a much more complex brain, with public access, would change how circuit questions are asked.
ocar.challenge: Imaging, aligning, segmenting, finding synapses, and proofreading at this scale, then defining cell types from connectivity as well as morphology and keeping an evolving dataset usable, had not been demonstrated for a large fraction of the fly central brain.
ocar.action: Xu, Januszewski, Scheffer, Plaza, and the FlyEM–Google collaboration summarize new methods and present circuitry for a large fraction of the adult Drosophila melanogaster central brain. Proofreading used NeuTu and Neu3, prioritizing fragments that most change connectivity and focusing extra completeness on the central complex and mushroom body. Brain regions were drawn from synapse density, glia, tracts, and wiring.
ocar.resolution: The preprint announces a public website and resources for exploring an exhaustive cell-type atlas, detailed central-brain circuits, and compartment statistics, aimed at experts and non-specialists. It states that companion papers will treat the hemibrain reconstruction, the central complex, and the mushroom body in more depth.
ocar.future_work: The note itself defers extensive analysis to those forthcoming papers. Highest completeness is still concentrated in biologically prioritized regions rather than uniformly across the volume.

summaries.beginner: This preprint announces a public wiring map of a large part of the adult fruit-fly central brain. It is the methods-and-data release that later companion papers analyze in more biological depth.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Xu, Januszewski, Scheffer, Plaza, and colleagues (FlyEM at Janelia with Google) present a dense connectome for a large fraction of the adult Drosophila central brain. They describe preparation through proofreading, connectivity-aware cell typing, and region annotation from synapse density, glia, tracts, and wiring. Completeness was pushed first in the central complex and mushroom body. A public site is meant to make partner identity and regional circuitry a lookup; deeper papers on hemibrain, central complex, and mushroom body are promised.
summaries.advanced: This is a January 2020 announcement preprint, not the later eLife analysis paper. Completeness still varies by region after higher-level proofreading of main branches and stronger pathways. Substructures such as layers and slices in central complex and mushroom body are described as often imprecise for lack of landmarks. Biological interpretation is explicitly deferred.

plain_language_summary: This preprint announces a public wiring map of a large part of the adult fruit-fly central brain. It is the methods-and-data release that later companion papers analyze in more biological depth.

ocar.opportunity: Flexible, long-timescale behaviors are thought to use recurrent networks in deep brain regions. In insects, the central complex (CX) supports directed locomotion, sleep, and context- and experience-dependent navigation, but a complete synaptic map had been missing.
ocar.challenge: Deep circuits are hard to interpret because inputs and outputs are usually difficult to identify, and attractor dynamics and vector computations are thought to depend on structured recurrence rather than simple sensory-to-motor chains.
ocar.action: Hulse, Haberkern, Franconville, Turner-Evans, Jayaraman, and colleagues report the first complete electron-microscopy connectome of the Drosophila CX, including all its neurons and circuits at synaptic resolution, from the hemibrain volume.
ocar.resolution: They identify new CX neuron types, sensory and motor pathways, and network motifs argued to extract head direction, maintain it with attractor dynamics, and combine it with other sensorimotor information for vector-based navigation, plus pathways that may select CX-driven actions by context and internal state.
ocar.future_work: Many proposed computations remain models. The authors treat a 90° PFN phase shift and excitatory LNO types as simplifying assumptions, note unknown functional significance of type-to-type phase variability, and leave the information carried by nodulus inputs to be determined.

summaries.beginner: Flies steer, sleep, and navigate using a deep midline brain region called the central complex. This paper maps every neuron and chemical synapse in that region so the loops that could hold a heading and pick an action can be read from the wiring.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (updated 2021; 2020 preprint), Hulse, Haberkern, Franconville, Turner-Evans, Jayaraman, and colleagues present a complete synaptic connectome of the adult Drosophila central complex. They report new cell types and motifs proposed to support head-direction extraction, attractor maintenance, and vector navigation, and pathways that may gate CX-driven behavior by context and state. Discussion of PFN phase shifts treats a precise 90° shift and excitatory LNO input as working assumptions for forward models of coordinate transformation.
summaries.advanced: Completeness is for CX neurons and synapses in this EM volume, not a demonstration that the motifs implement the named computations in vivo. Phase-shift and LNO-sign assumptions are explicit simplifications; vΔ and hΔ columnar variability is likewise reduced to keep-or-flip-by-180° in the models. Rotational-velocity content of nodulus input is described as still unknown.

plain_language_summary: Flies steer, sleep, and navigate using a deep midline brain region called the central complex. This paper maps every neuron and chemical synapse in that region so the loops that could hold a heading and pick an action can be read from the wiring.

ocar.opportunity: A motor neuron can play different dynamical roles in different behaviors without rewiring. Joint functional imaging and synaptic anatomy in the same specimen can show how converging pathways support that flexibility.
ocar.challenge: No current technology comprehensively records activity and reconstructs synapses in brains the size of a mouse or human. Even in smaller systems, obtaining both from the same tissue remains rare.
ocar.action: Ashaber, Tomina, Kassraian, Wagenaar, and colleagues recorded most neurons in a medicinal-leech segmental ganglion with a voltage-sensitive dye during fictive swimming, crawling, and local-bend escape, then imaged the same ganglion with serial block-face electron microscopy. They traced motor neuron DE-3 and all of its presynaptic partners to their somata.
ocar.resolution: Input synapses important for all of the behaviors were widely distributed over DE-3's branches, yet functional synapse clusters differed during fictive swimming versus crawling. Data are released publicly.
ocar.future_work: The reconstruction is a proof of concept centered on one motor neuron rather than a complete ganglion connectome; extending tracing and matching more functional assemblies is the obvious next step.

summaries.beginner: One leech motor neuron helps swimming, crawling, and a local escape bend without changing its wiring. This paper records the ganglion's activity, then traces that cell's incoming synapses in the electron microscope to see how the same anatomy supports different jobs.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Ashaber, Tomina, Kassraian, Ellisman, Wagenaar, and colleagues combined voltage-sensitive dye imaging of a medicinal-leech (Hirudo verbana) segmental ganglion during fictive swimming, crawling, and local bending with serial block-face EM of the same ganglion. They fully traced dorsal excitor motor neuron DE-3 and all of its presynaptic partners. Synapses used in all behaviors were spread over DE-3's arbor, but spatial clusters of co-active inputs differed between swimming and crawling.
summaries.advanced: The EM reconstruction is thorough for DE-3 and its presynaptic partners, not for every neuron in the ganglion. Behaviors are fictive motor patterns. Clustering results depend on chosen neighborhood parameters (tables explore several (dNN, dext) settings). Catalog organism tags that list mouse do not match the leech specimen in the paper.

plain_language_summary: One leech motor neuron helps swimming, crawling, and a local escape bend without changing its wiring. This paper records the ganglion's activity, then traces that cell's incoming synapses in the electron microscope to see how the same anatomy supports different jobs.

ocar.opportunity: How synaptic partners recognize each other and set appropriate connection numbers during embryonic development is a route to understanding circuit assembly. Comparative connectomics after experimental perturbations can separate identity, place, and activity.
ocar.challenge: The relative roles of partner identity, axon-terminal location, and developmental activity in setting synapse numbers, excitation–inhibition balance, and behavior are poorly resolved at synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Valdes-Aleman, Zlatic, Cardona, and colleagues combined electron-microscopy reconstruction, functional imaging, and behavior in the embryonic Drosophila nerve cord. They shifted partner axons to ectopic locations or silenced them and compared connectivity and function with controls.
ocar.resolution: Postsynaptic cells still found and connected to partners that had been moved or silenced. Orderly positioning and synaptic activity were nonetheless required for appropriate synapse numbers between specific partners, for excitation–inhibition balance, and for normal functional connectivity and behavior.
ocar.future_work: The study is grounded in identified mechanosensory and downstream cell types in the larval nerve cord; whether the same weighting of identity, location, and activity holds in other circuits or stages is not established here.

summaries.beginner: Developing fly neurons can still find their partners even if those partners sit in the wrong place or are quiet. This paper shows that getting the right number of connections, and therefore the right behavior, still depends on location and on activity during development.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (January 2021), Valdes-Aleman, Fetter, Cardona, Zlatic, and colleagues used EM reconstruction, calcium imaging, and behavior in the embryonic Drosophila nerve cord. Partners connected even when axons were shifted ectopically or silenced. Correct synapse numbers, excitation–inhibition balance, functional connectivity, and behavior nonetheless required orderly terminal positioning and developmental synaptic activity.
summaries.advanced: Connectivity is scored as fraction of postsynaptic input and compared with chi-square tests; calcium and behavior use rank-sum, chi-square, and t tests as specified in STAR Methods. The result is circuit-specific (mechanosensory partners including Basin and A08a) rather than a universal assembly rule. Silencing and ectopic-shift experiments do not imply that identity cues are unnecessary—only that they are not sufficient for proper numbers and function.

plain_language_summary: Developing fly neurons can still find their partners even if those partners sit in the wrong place or are quiet. This paper shows that getting the right number of connections, and therefore the right behavior, still depends on location and on activity during development.

ocar.opportunity: Sensory, local, projection, and motor neurons are the building blocks of circuits, but those classes must be split into cell types with known synapses. A complete inventory of second-order olfactory projection neurons would give holotypes for a model system.
ocar.challenge: Even in Drosophila, circuitry beyond the second olfactory layer is much less known than antennal-lobe logic. Light-level studies likely undercount projection neurons and cannot resolve axo-axonic and feedback motifs.
ocar.action: Bates, Schlegel, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstructed, in a whole-adult-brain EM volume, the full set of olfactory projection neurons from antennal lobe to higher centers, linking morphologies to the literature as synaptic-resolution holotypes.
ocar.resolution: They report 346 such projection neurons, about twice as many as light-level counts, and finalize 51 olfactory glomeruli. Types are stereotyped but not identical in cell and synapse number across hemispheres; some uniglomerular types vary by up to 50% (for example 2 versus 4 VA1d cells) in about 17% of cases, with axonal synapse totals often compensated. The lateral horn is the main target and contains hierarchical axo-axonic PN networks plus local-neuron and memory-related feedback; the mushroom-body calyx is organized differently.
ocar.future_work: The reconstructions are holotypes from one brain; whether numerical compensation and axo-axonic communities are identical in other individuals remains to be tested in additional volumes.

summaries.beginner: Smell information leaves the fly's antennal lobe on projection neurons headed for higher brain centers. This paper traces all of those cells in an electron-microscope whole brain and finds about twice as many as light microscopy had suggested.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Bates, Schlegel, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstruct a complete inventory of 346 adult Drosophila olfactory projection neurons in a whole-brain EM volume. Uniglomerular types can differ by up to 50% in cell number between hemispheres in about 17% of types, yet total axonal synapse counts can match, as for DA1 and DA2. New motifs in the lateral horn include axo-axonic PN communities and feedback onto PN axons, unlike the mushroom-body calyx.
summaries.advanced: Counts and motifs come from one EM brain (Zheng et al. volume). Multiglomerular PNs are numerous but have fewer axonal output synapses than uniglomerular PNs, so influence as individual feedforward units may be limited. Hemisphere compensation is shown for selected types, not proven as a universal rule. Functional roles of the axo-axonic hierarchy are inferred from anatomy.

plain_language_summary: Smell information leaves the fly's antennal lobe on projection neurons headed for higher brain centers. This paper traces all of those cells in an electron-microscope whole brain and finds about twice as many as light microscopy had suggested.

ocar.opportunity: Animals have innate and learned preferences for temperature and humidity, but the central circuits are far less mapped than olfaction. A whole-brain EM volume lets first-, second-, and third-order thermo- and hygrosensory neurons be reconstructed together.
ocar.challenge: Antennal thermo- and hygrosensory neurons target ventroposterior (VP) glomeruli whose full projection-neuron set, higher-order partners, and integration with olfaction and the clock were incomplete.
ocar.action: Marin, Roberts, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstructed VP glomeruli and their projection neurons in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume, then densely mapped neurons downstream of heating- and cooling-responsive PNs in the mushroom-body lateral accessory calyx (lACA).
ocar.resolution: They add two VP glomeruli to the five known (suggesting VP1l cool/cooling and VP1m humidity pending physiology), reconstruct 19 novel VP PN types, and show that a few Kenyon cells are purely thermosensory while most mix olfactory and thermo- or hygrosensory input. The lACA is a hub including DN1 clock neurons; a descending neuron mainly postsynaptic to dry-responsive VP PNs implies as few as two synapses from hygrosensory input to nerve-cord motor neurons.
ocar.future_work: Valence and function of novel glomeruli and PN types need physiology and sparse driver lines. Specific DAN/MBON partners of lACA Kenyon cells, and partners of lACA output neurons, remain unidentified.

summaries.beginner: Flies sense heat, cold, and humidity with antenna cells that look a lot like smell cells. This paper traces those pathways through the brain and finds a temperature hub that even talks to the circadian clock.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Marin, Jefferis, and colleagues reconstruct thermo- and hygrosensory circuitry in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume. They identify two additional VP glomeruli, 19 novel VP projection-neuron types, and a connectome of the lateral accessory calyx. A few α'/β' Kenyon cells receive only thermosensory input; DN1a and DN1p clock neurons innervate the lACA. A descending neuron fed mainly by dry-responsive VP PNs sits two synapses from hygrosensory afferents toward the nerve cord.
summaries.advanced: Novel glomeruli VP1l and VP1m are assigned cool/humidity roles from receptor expression, not from recordings in this paper. Average sensory-neuron counts per VP glomerulus are about one-quarter of olfactory glomeruli; many VP PNs are biglomerular. Integration hypotheses (pooling similar valences in PNs, mixing at third order) are anatomical. The two-synapse claim is a shortest anatomical path, not a demonstrated motor reflex.

plain_language_summary: Flies sense heat, cold, and humidity with antenna cells that look a lot like smell cells. This paper traces those pathways through the brain and finds a temperature hub that even talks to the circadian clock.

ocar.opportunity: Automated acquisition and analysis put whole-brain connectomes of 100,000 or more neurons on the horizon. An open, browser-based community could distribute proofreading worldwide and share edits immediately.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading whole-brain automated reconstructions will still take many person-years. Tools must scale socially as well as computationally, and closed 'walled gardens' slow discovery.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, McKellar, Seung, Murthy, and colleagues present FlyWire: collaborative 3D editing of a spatially chunked supervoxel graph in the browser, with programmatic access to edit history, applied to a Drosophila melanogaster whole-brain EM volume. They demonstrate circuit analysis on reconstructed mechanosensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: Mean backbone proofreading time is about 19 minutes per neuron; at an estimate of about 100,000 cells, backbone proofreading with existing twigs and automatic synapses would take about 16 person-years. At writing, more than 160 researchers from more than 40 labs had been trained. Completeness across both hemispheres lets partners of a neuron be identified brain-wide.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect remaining errors to fall with better segmentation and with automatic likely-error detection. They propose species-wide crowdsourcing so labs prioritize their own circuits to the accuracy their questions need.

summaries.beginner: A whole fly brain is too big for one lab to correct by hand. FlyWire is a website where people anywhere can jointly fix an automated tracing and see one another's edits.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2022), Dorkenwald, McKellar, Seung, Murthy, and colleagues introduce FlyWire, a browser-based community for proofreading a Drosophila whole-brain EM segmentation via a chunked supervoxel graph. They reconstruct mechanosensory neurons to show circuit analysis. They estimate about 19 minutes of backbone proofreading per neuron and about 16 person-years for ~100,000 cells with automatic synapses. Membership exceeded 160 researchers in more than 40 labs at the time of writing.
summaries.advanced: The 16 person-year figure is a backbone-plus-existing-twigs estimate, not a finished whole-brain connectome. Competing interests note that some authors own or work at Zetta AI. Accuracy of the live segmentation is improving by construction; analyses here are of a snapshot. Social scaling assumes the Drosophila community's sharing norms transfer.

plain_language_summary: A whole fly brain is too big for one lab to correct by hand. FlyWire is a website where people anywhere can jointly fix an automated tracing and see one another's edits.

ocar.opportunity: The hemibrain connectome supplies morphology and synapses for much of the adult fly central brain. A full olfactory annotation, from sensory neurons to descending interneurons, can turn that graph into a usable sensory system map.
ocar.challenge: Extracting information flow and layered organization from a dense connectome of this size, and measuring how stereotyped morphology and connectivity are across brains, required new tools and a second dataset.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Bates, Jefferis, and colleagues annotated all first-order, second-order, and lateral-horn-associated third-order olfactory neurons in the hemibrain. They developed graph methods to map layers from olfactory input to descending interneurons and compared neurons across two brains (three hemispheres).
ocar.resolution: They report motifs including highly lateralized antennal-lobe circuits and convergence downstream of mushroom body and lateral horn. Morphology is strikingly similar across brains; connectivity correlates with morphology, and neurons of the same morphological type show similar connection variability within one brain as across two brains. They release R and Python packages (neuprintr, hemibrainr, navis, and others).
ocar.future_work: Layer analysis is proposed for other modalities and for planned male and female CNS volumes. Comparative connectomics across more individuals is only begun.

summaries.beginner: This paper turns the fly hemibrain wiring map into a full tour of the smell system, from sensors to cells that leave the brain. It also checks how similar those cells are in a second fly.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Schlegel, Bates, Jefferis, and colleagues annotate the complete hemibrain olfactory system through lateral-horn third-order neurons and extract layered information flow to descending interneurons. Motifs include lateralized antennal-lobe circuits and downstream convergence after mushroom body and lateral horn. Comparing two brains (three hemispheres), morphological types match closely; connection variability within a type is similar inside one brain and across brains. Supporting software is released in the natverse ecosystem.
summaries.advanced: The hemibrain is roughly 25,000 neurons and 20 million synapses, about half the central brain of one fly, so 'full' olfactory coverage is within that volume plus a second FAFB-style dataset for stereotypy. Functional hypotheses (stereo odor processing, feedback control) are connectome-derived. Cross-brain comparison is three hemispheres, not a population study.

plain_language_summary: This paper turns the fly hemibrain wiring map into a full tour of the smell system, from sensors to cells that leave the brain. It also checks how similar those cells are in a second fly.

ocar.opportunity: Growing electron-microscopy connectomics volumes make storage, retrieval, and interactive viewing of images and segmentations a bottleneck for analysis and sharing.
ocar.challenge: Researchers need to fetch layers of images and segments by spatial location with low latency, store multiresolution imagery and large numbers of objects, and do so in a way that other software or public databases could reuse.
ocar.action: Yuan, Shen, Han, and colleagues built a server module on Hadoop and HBase with pyramid image storage and block storage of volume segmentations, plus a spatial location-based retrieval method they report as constant time complexity. The client uses a three-level image cache.
ocar.resolution: They report real-time performance on large-scale tests and argue the server can back other tools or a public shared database. Segmentation objects are stored as primitives with attributes such as ids, types, centroids, color, and connections.
ocar.future_work: Cache area cannot grow without bound; multithreading is used to improve cache efficiency. Broader adoption as a community backend is proposed rather than demonstrated across many labs.

summaries.beginner: Connectomics volumes are so large that just storing and fetching the pictures becomes its own problem. This paper describes a server and browser cache built so researchers can jump around huge electron-microscope stacks without waiting.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Sciences (2020), Yuan, Zhang, Shen, Han, and colleagues present a Hadoop/HBase data-management module for connectome reconstruction. Electron-microscopy images are stored as resolution pyramids and segmentations as blocks, with spatial queries they describe as constant-time. A three-level client cache reduces fetch latency. The server is pitched as reusable infrastructure for other software or shared databases.
summaries.advanced: Performance claims are from the authors' tests as summarized in the paper; independent benchmarks and dataset sizes in production FlyEM-scale settings are not given in the selected extract. The design stores contours/primitives rather than raw voxels for segments, which helps display but is a representational choice. This is infrastructure, not a new biological reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Connectomics volumes are so large that just storing and fetching the pictures becomes its own problem. This paper describes a server and browser cache built so researchers can jump around huge electron-microscope stacks without waiting.

ocar.opportunity: New EM reconstructions of animals such as Drosophila contain tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of connections and interest non-specialists. A queryable database can make those graphs usable.
ocar.challenge: Earlier reconstructions were small enough that domain experts and ad hoc tools sufficed. Scale, evolving proofreading, quality assessment, and mixed user skill now require a different data model.
ocar.action: Clements, Plaza, and colleagues introduce neuPrint: a neo4j graph database with Cypher queries, a biological data model at multiple abstractions, batch and incremental updates, quality tools, a web interface, and a programmer API. They demonstrate queries including reconstruction-incompleteness of a neuron's outputs and type lookup by regular expression.
ocar.resolution: They report that the database supports diverse queries on millions of synaptic connections. Unlike atlas projects that compile many smaller datasets, neuPrint emphasizes access to specific expensive EM volumes.
ocar.future_work: They plan to add subcellular organelles to the data model as automatic extraction becomes more reliable.

summaries.beginner: A fly connectome is a huge list of cells and the synapses between them. neuPrint is a database and website that lets biologists ask graph questions of that list without writing a custom pipeline.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Clements, Dolafi, Scheffer, Plaza, and colleagues describe neuPrint, a neo4j/Cypher ecosystem for EM connectomes. It stores neurons and connections at several abstractions, supports proofreading-era incremental updates and quality checks, and offers both a web UI and APIs. Example queries recover output reconstruction status distributions and neuron-type counts. The design targets one large volume rather than a multi-study atlas.
summaries.advanced: Effectiveness is shown with example queries and a claim of millions of synaptic connections, not a timed bake-off against other graph stores in the selected extract. Canonical-atlas comparison is philosophical: neuPrint is dataset-specific by design. Organelle support is future work. The hemibrain deployment is the intended production context but is not fully benchmarked here.

plain_language_summary: A fly connectome is a huge list of cells and the synapses between them. neuPrint is a database and website that lets biologists ask graph questions of that list without writing a custom pipeline.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes reconstruct morphology and synapses but usually lack synaptic sign. If transmitter type can be read from micrographs, putative excitation and inhibition can be added to whole-brain graphs.
ocar.challenge: Transmitter identity is not labeled in standard EM. Co-transmission, peptides, receptors, and gap junctions further complicate inferring functional sign from a single predicted small-molecule transmitter.
ocar.action: Eckstein, Bates, Funke, Jefferis, and colleagues train artificial neural networks to classify transmitters from synaptic electron micrographs in Drosophila, apply an explainability method, and predict transmitters across two connectomes.
ocar.resolution: The network discriminates six transmitters (acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, octopamine) at 87% accuracy per synapse and 94% per neuron on average. Hemilineages largely express one fast-acting transmitter. Explainable features reveal ultrastructural differences among classical transmitters. Predicted classes differ in features such as polarization and projection targets.
ocar.future_work: The authors list misprediction (including co- and alternative transmission), other transmitters (histamine, tyramine, glycine, nitric oxide, and many neuropeptides), monoaminergic and peptidergic co-transmission, receptors, and gap junctions as unsolved. Serotonin was the weakest class; some known neuropeptidergic neurons were predicted serotonergic.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of fly synapses carry clues to which chemical a cell uses. This paper trains a network to guess six transmitters so wiring diagrams can be given plus and minus signs.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2024), Eckstein, Bates, Funke, Jefferis, and colleagues predict acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, and octopamine from Drosophila synaptic EM, with average accuracies of 87% at synapses and 94% at whole neurons. Explainable AI highlights ultrastructural differences among classical transmitters. Applied to whole-brain connectomes, predictions indicate that hemilineages usually share one fast-acting transmitter and that transmitter classes differ in morphology and targets.
summaries.advanced: Accuracy is not uniform; serotonin is the weakest, and some large peptidergic cells are called serotonergic. Transmitter identity is not the same as synaptic sign (receptors, co-transmission, peptides, and gap junctions are listed as missing). Ground truth and application span FAFB/FlyWire-scale resources; catalog metadata listing 2020 bioRxiv understate the 2024 Cell version used here.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of fly synapses carry clues to which chemical a cell uses. This paper trains a network to guess six transmitters so wiring diagrams can be given plus and minus signs.

ocar.opportunity: Dense EM connectivity lacks molecular and functional labels. Fluorescent immunohistochemistry of key proteins could add cell-type and synapse identity if it can be done before en bloc volume EM.
ocar.challenge: Detergent permeabilization, normally required for antibody penetration in thick sections, destroys ultrastructure needed for FIB-SEM, GCIB-SEM, or SBEM. Post-sectioning methods such as array tomography are incompatible with those en bloc pipelines.
ocar.action: Fulton and Briggman omit permeabilization and instead preserve extracellular space during fixation so antibodies can travel in thick mouse sections. They label neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins across hundreds of microns in multiple regions, then perform proof-of-principle two-photon imaging followed by 3D EM.
ocar.resolution: Permeabilization-free labeling works in hippocampus, olfactory bulb, and other regions while retaining reconstructable ultrastructure and identifiable synapses. The authors argue antibodies may need to cross only one membrane from preserved ECS, perhaps via aldehyde semi-permeabilization or rare damage.
ocar.future_work: The membrane-crossing mechanism remains unclear. They suggest trying high-pressure frozen tissue with more native ECS. The correlative experiments are proof of principle, not a production multimodal volume.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot tell you which proteins a cell or synapse contains. This paper stains thick mouse brain slices without punching holes in membranes, so the same tissue can still be imaged in the electron microscope.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Fulton and Briggman describe permeabilization-free en bloc immunohistochemistry in extracellular-space-preserved mouse sections hundreds of microns thick. They label NeuN, calbindin/calretinin, synaptic proteins, and genetically encoded probes in hippocampus, olfactory bulb, and other regions, then combine two-photon protein maps with 3D EM. Ultrastructure remains adequate to reconstruct neurons and identify synapses.
summaries.advanced: How IgG (hydrodynamic radius about 5 nm) crosses an unpermeabilized membrane is unknown; aldehyde denaturation or undetected membrane damage are speculated. Compatibility is argued for FIB-SEM, GCIB-SEM, and SBEM rather than demonstrated at petascale. Catalog dataset tags pointing at MICrONS are not required to interpret this methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot tell you which proteins a cell or synapse contains. This paper stains thick mouse brain slices without punching holes in membranes, so the same tissue can still be imaged in the electron microscope.

ocar.opportunity: Limb motor circuits live in the insect ventral nerve cord, homologous to spinal cord but more accessible. A synapse-resolution VNC volume would let sensory feedback onto motor neurons be read directly.
ocar.challenge: Manual serial-section pickup for TEM is slow and lossy; high-throughput SEM can be expensive or slow. Affordable automated TEM at VNC scale was needed.
ocar.action: Maniates-Selvin, Hildebrand, Graham, Lee, and colleagues developed GridTape—automated section collection on slotted tape plus automated TEM—and acquired a synapse-resolution volume of an adult female Drosophila VNC. They reconstructed 507 motor neurons, including all leg and wing motor neurons.
ocar.resolution: A class of leg sensory neurons (campaniform sensilla) synapses directly onto the largest-caliber motor axons on both sides of the body, a candidate fast feedback pathway. Dataset, reconstructions registered to a standard atlas, and GridTape designs and software are released. They argue ten TEMCA-GT systems can be built for the price of one commercial multi-beam SEM.
ocar.future_work: Faster cameras, brighter sources, wider tape, and beam-scanning are proposed. The authors highlight multi-individual comparisons (development, dimorphism, plasticity, disease) as newly practical if imaging is cheaper.

summaries.beginner: The fly's ventral nerve cord is the analog of a spinal cord, running the legs and wings. This paper describes a tape-based electron-microscope pipeline that imaged a whole female cord and found a direct sensory shortcut onto big motor axons.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Maniates-Selvin, Hildebrand, Graham, Tuthill, Lee, and colleagues introduce GridTape automated serial-section TEM and a female adult Drosophila VNC volume. They reconstruct 507 motor neurons, covering legs and wings, and report monosynaptic input from a proprioceptor class onto the largest motor axons bilaterally. Open data are registered to a light-microscopy atlas; hardware designs are shared to lower cost relative to multi-beam SEM.
summaries.advanced: The dataset is one female VNC, not a brain-plus-cord connectome. Sensory–motor conclusions concern a specific campaniform pathway, not all proprioceptors. Cost comparisons (ten TEMCA-GTs versus one multi-beam SEM; about USD $4 per slot for support film) are authors' estimates. Slot size (2 × 1.5 mm in the text) limits sample geometry without further engineering.

plain_language_summary: The fly's ventral nerve cord is the analog of a spinal cord, running the legs and wings. This paper describes a tape-based electron-microscope pipeline that imaged a whole female cord and found a direct sensory shortcut onto big motor axons.

ocar.opportunity: Dopaminergic neurons drive learning across animals, but the circuits that set their activity, and thus what is learned, are poorly mapped. The larval Drosophila mushroom body is small enough for a complete upstream connectome.
ocar.challenge: How aversive and appetitive memory compartments interact, and whether feedback onto DANs computes integrated predictions, was not known at synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Fushiki, Cardona, Zlatic, Litwin-Kumar, and colleagues reconstructed all neurons presynaptic to mushroom-body dopaminergic neurons in a larval EM volume, combined that map with functional tests of DANs and their partners, and modeled the motifs on learning tasks.
ocar.resolution: They find 61 feedback neuron pairs providing one- and/or two-step MBON-to-modulatory feedback; many DANs receive more than 50% of dendritic input from these pathways, often linking aversive and appetitive systems. Modeling indicates the motifs increase flexibility and performance. Direct MBON-to-DAN contacts exist but indirect routes via feedback neurons are prominent.
ocar.future_work: Adult Drosophila has some known MBON–DAN links; how larval motifs scale to the adult MB is only partly addressed by citation. Code and CATMAID reconstructions are released for further task-specific modeling.

summaries.beginner: Learning in the fly larva depends on dopamine cells that tell the mushroom body what was good or bad. This paper maps every neuron that talks to those dopamine cells and finds a thick web of feedback from the memory outputs themselves.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2020), Eschbach, Fushiki, Litwin-Kumar, Cardona, Zlatic, and colleagues reconstruct the circuitry upstream of all dopaminergic neurons in the Drosophila larval mushroom body. Sixty-one feedback neuron pairs carry one- or two-step MBON-to-DAN signals; many DANs get more than half their dendritic synapses from feedback, often bridging aversive and appetitive compartments. Functional experiments and a circuit model argue these motifs support integrated predictions and improve learning-task performance.
summaries.advanced: The connectome is larval, not adult. The >50% dendritic-input figure is for many—not all—modulatory neurons. Model gains are computational (Fig. 7), not a proof that larvae use the same objective. Imaging and behavior analysis code for some figures is available only on request, while connectivity matrices are released.

plain_language_summary: Learning in the fly larva depends on dopamine cells that tell the mushroom body what was good or bad. This paper maps every neuron that talks to those dopamine cells and finds a thick web of feedback from the memory outputs themselves.

ocar.opportunity: Kenyon cells transform broadly tuned, stereotyped olfactory projection-neuron input into sparse, nonstereotyped codes thought to support associative memory. Whether that expansion is random had not been testable at synaptic scale.
ocar.challenge: Theory and earlier experiments suggested random PN-to-KC connectivity, but mapping enough synapses for a fair test against defined null models was hard. Prior samples may have lacked statistical power.
ocar.action: Zheng, Bock, and colleagues mapped large numbers of PN-to-KC synapses in a whole-brain Drosophila EM volume, compared the graph with null models, related structure to axonal geometry in the main calyx, and simulated discrimination.
ocar.resolution: A community of food-responsive PN types converges onto individual KCs more often than chance, matching nearby axonal territories in the calyx. Models of the observed wiring discriminate food-related PN combinations better than others, which the authors call an olfactory 'associative fovea'. The same PN community appears in lateral-horn axo-axonic networks (Bates et al.). Downsampling to Caron et al. 2013 sample sizes makes the community undetectable.
ocar.future_work: Ipsilateral-plus-contralateral completion in FAFB, additional brains (e.g. hemibrain), genetic background, activity, and developmental environment are listed as tests of conservation. Even if structure is shared, MBON odor responses remain highly individual (Hige et al.).

summaries.beginner: Fly memory cells were thought to sample smells at random. This electron-microscope map finds that food-related smell channels share Kenyon cells more often than chance, as if the memory center spends extra resolution on meals.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Zheng, Li, Bock, and colleagues reconstruct many projection-neuron-to-Kenyon-cell synapses in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume. Food-responsive PN types converge on KCs above null expectation, consistent with clustered axons in the main calyx. Network models discriminate those PN combinations better than others. The community matches a food-related PN clique in the lateral horn and disappears if the sample is reduced to earlier study sizes.
summaries.advanced: The map is not a complete bilateral PN-to-KC connectome. Random-expansion theory is not discarded globally—only a detectable food-related bias is added. Functional 'fovea' claims come from simplified discrimination models, not behavior. Conservation across individuals is inferred from light-level axon territories, not multiple EM brains in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Fly memory cells were thought to sample smells at random. This electron-microscope map finds that food-related smell channels share Kenyon cells more often than chance, as if the memory center spends extra resolution on meals.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit models need connection strengths, which are costly to measure physiologically. If morphological synapse counts predict contact area, and area tracks strength, connectomes can supply usable weights.
ocar.challenge: Most connectomic studies use synapse counts as a proxy, but the quantitative link to synaptic surface area across transmitters and cell types was not established in Drosophila.
ocar.action: Barnes, Bonnéry, and Cardona measured synaptic counts and synaptic surface area from volume EM of the larval Drosophila central nervous system across a variety of neurotransmitters and edge types (sensory axons onto excitatory interneurons; inhibitory interneurons onto excitatory interneurons).
ocar.resolution: Total synaptic surface area from one presynaptic neuron to one postsynaptic neuron is accurately predicted from contact number alone, independent of participating cell types in the studied set. Combined with prior reports that area tracks strength, this supports using counts (or input fractions) in models.
ocar.future_work: Whether the correlation holds as arbors grow (counts increase about five-fold from first to third instar while input fractions stay stable) is argued by analogy but not remeasured across stages here. Other edge types and the adult are extrapolations.

summaries.beginner: Connectome papers usually count synapses and treat bigger counts as stronger connections. This study checks that shortcut in the fly larva and finds that contact number does predict total contact area.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2022), Barnes, Bonnéry, and Cardona compare morphological synapse counts with summed synaptic surface area in larval Drosophila volume EM. Across several transmitters and both excitatory and inhibitory edge types, total area from a given pre- to postsynaptic neuron is predicted from count alone. They argue this justifies count-based weights used in prior circuit models, while noting input fractions may be preferable when comparing growing arbors.
summaries.advanced: The result is for studied larval CNS connections, not a proof that Peters' rule (apposition predicts synapses) holds—the authors note Peters' rule fails where tested. Strength is inferred via published area–strength linearity, not physiology in this dataset. Developmental invariance is inferred from published five-fold growth with stable fractions, not a longitudinal EM series here. Catalog year 2020 reflects the preprint era; the PDF is the 2022 article.

plain_language_summary: Connectome papers usually count synapses and treat bigger counts as stronger connections. This study checks that shortcut in the fly larva and finds that contact number does predict total contact area.

ocar.opportunity: The mushroom body has a conserved architecture, a dense connectome, and a rich experimental literature on learning and memory, so it is a test bed for reading computation from synapses.
ocar.challenge: How sensory modalities reach Kenyon cells and MBONs, how DANs modulate that transfer, how MB outputs integrate with the central complex, and how DANs themselves are driven, including by MBON feedback, were incomplete even after hemibrain reconstruction.
ocar.action: Li, Rubin, and colleagues analyze the adult Drosophila mushroom body in hemibrain:v1.1 via neuPrint, combining connectivity with prior cell-type physiology and behavior.
ocar.resolution: They report extensive visual input, MBONs with direct descending-neuron connections, unexpected structure in sensory inputs and in modality transfer to MBONs, DAN modulation of that transfer, MB–central-complex links, and DAN input including MBON feedback. They analogize MB teaching signals to climbing-fiber-like events in cerebellum-like systems.
ocar.future_work: Unanticipated motifs are explicitly framed as hypotheses for cell-type-specific physiology, plasticity rules, consolidation, and internal-state effects now that driver lines and whole-brain imaging exist.

summaries.beginner: The fly mushroom body is the brain's famous learning center. This paper reads its complete wiring map and finds extra visual input, shortcuts to descending neurons, and feedback that could tell dopamine cells what has already been learned.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Li, Abbott, Litwin-Kumar, Waddell, Rubin, and colleagues analyze the adult Drosophila mushroom-body connectome in the hemibrain. New components include substantial visual input and MBONs that synapse directly onto descending neurons. They describe structured sensory innervation, modality-specific routes to MBONs, dopaminergic modulation of those routes, MB–central-complex connectivity, and MBON feedback onto DANs. The map is offered as a foundation for theory and experiment, with parallels to cerebellum-like teaching signals.
summaries.advanced: Analyses use hemibrain:v1.1; some figures apply synapse-number or percentage thresholds stated only in legends. Computational inferences from connectivity are not themselves behavioral proofs. The paper is an analysis of an existing volume, not a new EM acquisition. Comparison to cortex/hippocampus burst-driven plasticity is analogical.

plain_language_summary: The fly mushroom body is the brain's famous learning center. This paper reads its complete wiring map and finds extra visual input, shortcuts to descending neurons, and feedback that could tell dopamine cells what has already been learned.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level maps now let researchers infer circuit computations where anatomy, cell types, and behavior already intersect. The adult mushroom body is such a case.
ocar.challenge: Dense MB connectivity had not been fully interpreted for visual input, descending output, cross-modal structure, DAN modulation, central-complex coupling, and DAN afferents including MBON feedback.
ocar.action: Li, Rubin, and colleagues post a bioRxiv analysis of the adult Drosophila mushroom-body connectome covering the same themes later published in eLife: new components, sensory and DAN structure, output integration, and MB–CX links.
ocar.resolution: The preprint's narrative matches the later paper: extensive visual input, MBONs onto descending neurons, structured modality transfer, DAN modulation, and recurrent MBON–DAN motifs illustrated for appetitive memory (for example sugar-responsive DANs depressing odor-specific KC synapses in γ4, γ5, β′2, and β1, with hunger-sensitive MBON11 promoting approach configurations).
ocar.future_work: As in the journal version, motifs are hypotheses for experiment. This record is the August 2020 preprint, not a second independent reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: This preprint is the mushroom-body wiring analysis later published in eLife: a complete look at how the fly learning center is hooked up, including vision, dopamine, and paths out to behavior.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (August 2020), Li, Lindsey, Waddell, Rubin, and colleagues present the adult Drosophila mushroom-body connectome analysis that subsequently appeared in eLife. They highlight visual input, MBONs with descending targets, structured sensory and DAN organization, MB–central-complex connectivity, and MBON feedback onto DANs. Figure-level examples include an appetitive-memory schematic in which sugar-responsive DANs and hunger-sensitive MBON11 reconfigure approach versus avoidance outputs.
summaries.advanced: This is the same scientific project as the eLife MB paper, not a distinct dataset. Videos referenced in the preprint are not in the selected extract. Circuit diagrams (e.g. Fig. 41) are interpretive overlays on hemibrain connectivity. Prefer the peer-reviewed eLife version for citation unless the preprint-specific record is required.

plain_language_summary: This preprint is the mushroom-body wiring analysis later published in eLife: a complete look at how the fly learning center is hooked up, including vision, dopamine, and paths out to behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes constrain small circuits, but whether synapse-level structure predicts mesoscale functional connectivity across a whole central brain was open. Drosophila now offers both a dense connectome and whole-brain imaging.
ocar.challenge: Human MRI structure–function correlations are limited by coarse structural data. It was unclear how well resting-state regional correlations would match cell- and synapse-level anatomy, or whether indirect paths would matter.
ocar.action: Turner, Mann, and Clandinin combined Drosophila connectome data with whole-brain in vivo imaging of defined central-brain regions and compared direct and indirect anatomical pathways with resting-state functional connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Functional connectivity is strongly associated with direct and indirect anatomical strength. Mushroom body and central complex are more functionally coupled to the rest of the brain than direct connections predict. Synapse counts did not improve mesoscale prediction over cell-count connectivity (those two structural measures correlate at r = 0.90). The structural network shows small-world and scale-free signatures familiar from mammalian cortex.
ocar.future_work: Shortest-path distance is treated as a proxy for broader indirect connectedness; which higher-order paths matter is left open. Graph-embedding approaches from human imaging are suggested.

summaries.beginner: Does the fly's wiring diagram predict which brain regions rise and fall together at rest? This paper says yes, and that learning centers are even more in sync than their direct cables would suggest.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Turner, Mann, and Clandinin relate the Drosophila central-brain connectome to mesoscale resting-state functional connectivity from whole-brain imaging. Direct and indirect anatomical pathways both predict functional coupling; mushroom body and central complex exceed direct-connection predictions. Adding synapse counts does not raise the structure–function correlation beyond cell-count connectivity (r = 0.90 between those structural measures). Topology shares small-world and scale-free features with mammalian cortical networks.
summaries.advanced: Resting-state regional correlations average many neurons and are not a substitute for identified-cell physiology. The authors note the fly structure–function correlation exceeds typical human MRI coefficients for many reasons (resolution, completeness, biology). Indirect-path importance for MB and CX is correlational. The work uses the hemibrain-era connectome plus prior whole-brain imaging (Mann et al. 2017).

plain_language_summary: Does the fly's wiring diagram predict which brain regions rise and fall together at rest? This paper says yes, and that learning centers are even more in sync than their direct cables would suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Large projects in genomics and astronomy matter because they enable many later questions from the same rich data. Automated synapse-level mapping now makes complicated brain circuits similarly ripe for a community resource.
ocar.challenge: Whether the field should commit to mapping an entire mouse brain at synaptic resolution, and what unique benefits that would bring, remains a strategic question rather than a completed reconstruction.
ocar.action: Abbott, Bock, Lichtman, Seung, Svoboda, and many co-authors discuss, in Cell, the scientific case for a mouse brain connectome at the level of synapses.
ocar.resolution: They argue that such a map would function as a data-rich source for continuously arising questions, analogous to genomics and astronomy surveys, rather than answering only one pre-specified problem.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a perspective on benefits and motivation, not a methods or results paper; realizing a mouse-brain synapse map is left as a community goal.

summaries.beginner: Some scientific maps are valuable because they let people ask new questions for years. This Cell commentary argues that a synapse-level wiring diagram of a mouse brain would be that kind of map.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2020), Abbott, Bock, Callaway, Denk, Lichtman, Seung, Svoboda, Van Essen, and colleagues discuss benefits of mapping a mouse brain at synaptic resolution. They analogize connectomics to genomics and astronomy: influence comes from enabling many later analyses of one data-rich source. Automated mapping, they argue, has made complicated circuits ready for that treatment.
summaries.advanced: This card follows the published abstract: the bundled PDF extract is a different paper (a 2025 Current Protocols workflow for BossDB graphs) and was not used. The article is a perspective without a new volume, neuron count, or cost model in the abstract. No quantitative mouse-brain EM results are claimed here.

plain_language_summary: Some scientific maps are valuable because they let people ask new questions for years. This Cell commentary argues that a synapse-level wiring diagram of a mouse brain would be that kind of map.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroanatomy is now large-scale and quantitative. Researchers should not reimplement file I/O, neuron data structures, spatial transforms, or standard analyses for every project.
ocar.challenge: Users spend effort on documentation, dependencies, and hopping between analysis and visualization tools, and they need to compare morphology and connectivity after imaging or registration into shared templates and across light- and electron-microscopy modalities.
ocar.action: Bates, Manton, Jefferis, and colleagues present the natverse, a suite of interoperable open-source R packages for reading local and remote neuron data, visualization, clustering, graph-theoretic branching analyses, template bridging, and integration of most Drosophila light- and EM-connectomic datasets.
ocar.resolution: The toolkit supports comparison of many neurons in a common space, transformations between templates, and reuse of CRAN/Bioconductor infrastructure. Examples cover skeletons, volumes, synapses, NBLAST, Strahler order, pruning, and cell typing. Functions can be called from Python, Julia, or MATLAB. Code examples live at github.com/natverse/nat.examples.
ocar.future_work: The authors position natverse as a platform for community packages, analogous to Fiji or Bioconductor, rather than a finished catalog of every future dataset.

summaries.beginner: Fly brain maps now live in many different atlases and file formats. The natverse is a set of R tools that read those data, put them in one space, and compare shapes and connections without starting from scratch.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Bates, Manton, Jefferis, and colleagues describe the natverse, open-source R packages for neuroanatomy. Users can load local or remote skeletons and volumes, cluster and visualize neurons, run graph and NBLAST analyses, and transform between Drosophila light-microscopy and EM template spaces. The suite is meant to integrate most fly light and connectomic datasets and to be callable from other languages. Tutorials and example code are published with the paper.
summaries.advanced: The demonstration focus is Drosophila; other species depend on available templates and importers. This is software infrastructure, not a new connectome. Scale claims ('vast majority' of fly LM/EM datasets) are as of 2020 and will lag new resources unless packages are updated. Some advanced analyses still require writing R.

plain_language_summary: Fly brain maps now live in many different atlases and file formats. The natverse is a set of R tools that read those data, put them in one space, and compare shapes and connections without starting from scratch.

ocar.opportunity: Whitening—decorrelating activity patterns for later classification—is a fundamental computation. A functional connectome of a small olfactory bulb can test which wiring motifs implement it.
ocar.challenge: Mechanistic accounts need both odor-evoked activity and a complete wiring diagram in the same network. General topography or first-order cell-type statistics may not suffice.
ocar.action: Wanner and Friedrich recorded odor-evoked activity in a zebrafish larva olfactory bulb and then densely reconstructed the wiring diagram with volumetric electron microscopy. They compared observed motifs with simulations that lesioned or restored specific connections.
ocar.resolution: Multisynaptic motifs mediating reciprocal inhibition between similarly tuned neurons are overrepresented. That connectivity suppressed redundant responses and was necessary and sufficient to reproduce whitening in simulations. Decorrelation is described as selective inhibition of strongly active, correlation-promoting mitral-cell cohorts (contrast reduction), not contrast enhancement or IN–IN disinhibition.
ocar.future_work: How tuning-dependent mitral–interneuron–mitral connectivity develops (molecular versus activity-dependent) remains open; the larva was reconstructed before activity-dependent glomerular morphological effects reported elsewhere. Image and skeleton data are released via NeuroData and Zenodo.

summaries.beginner: The olfactory bulb cleans up overlapping smell patterns so they are easier to tell apart—a step called whitening. This zebrafish study pairs recordings with a complete electron-microscope wiring map and finds the trick in extra inhibition between cells that like the same odors.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2020), Wanner and Friedrich measured odor-evoked activity in a larval zebrafish olfactory bulb and reconstructed its complete wiring diagram with volumetric EM (1,022 neurons' skeletons are released). Overrepresented multisynaptic motifs implement reciprocal inhibition among similarly tuned cells. Simulations find those motifs necessary and sufficient for whitening; removing interneuron–interneuron connections does not explain decorrelation.
summaries.advanced: The preparation is one larva at a stage argued to precede activity-dependent glomerular morphological change, so adult or experience-dependent wiring may differ. Whitening is reproduced in simulations of this network, not in a causal in vivo lesion of the identified motifs. Input correlations are attributed to co-activated receptor groups; that chemical ecology is assumed, not re-derived here.

plain_language_summary: The olfactory bulb cleans up overlapping smell patterns so they are easier to tell apart—a step called whitening. This zebrafish study pairs recordings with a complete electron-microscope wiring map and finds the trick in extra inhibition between cells that like the same odors.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-body coordination of effectors is hard to study without a synaptic map of an entire animal. Beyond C. elegans and Ciona, few cellular-level whole-animal connectomes exist.
ocar.challenge: Annelid larvae have segmentally repeated ciliary bands, glands, pigment cells, and muscles whose intersegmental control was not fully charted at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Verasztó, Jékely, and colleagues reconstructed and annotated more than 1,500 neurons and 6,500 non-neuronal cells in a whole-body serial EM volume of a three-day Platynereis dumerilii nectochaete larva, classifying 180 neuronal and 90 non-neuronal types.
ocar.resolution: They analyze modular architecture and polysynaptic paths from 428 sensory neurons to ciliated cells, glands, pigment cells, and muscles. Intersegmental motoneurons (for example MNspinning to spinning glands, multi-segment muscle motoneurons, ciliomotor cells spanning bands) are candidates for coordinated recruitment. A companion paper will treat somatic musculature. New putative mechanosensors (SNblunt, SNFVa, SNbronto) are proposed from anatomy.
ocar.future_work: Transmitters are known for only a small fraction of neurons; gene-expression atlas registration failed on this volume because of fixation and alignment. Sensory function is known for few of 45 morphological sensory types. Crawling with intersegmental phase lags is not fully developed at three days.

summaries.beginner: This paper maps every cell in a three-segment marine worm larva, nerves and non-nerves alike. The wiring shows how sensors can reach cilia, glands, pigment, and muscle throughout the body.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Verasztó, Jasek, Jékely, and colleagues present a whole-animal connectome of a three-day Platynereis dumerilii larva: more than 1,500 neurons and 6,500 other cells, grouped into 180 neuronal and 90 non-neuronal types. They trace paths from 428 sensory neurons to four effector classes and highlight intersegmental motoneurons that could coordinate repeated organs. Musculature innervation is deferred to a companion paper.
summaries.advanced: The larva lacks palps, cirri, feeding, and visceral muscle; it is not an adult annelid. Neurotransmitters are mostly invisible to EM; immunogold maps some peptides. Atlas registration to a three-day gene-expression map did not succeed. Sensory functions for most of the 45 sensory types are unknown. Whole-animal comparisons are to C. elegans and Ciona, with Drosophila as CNS rather than whole-body.

plain_language_summary: This paper maps every cell in a three-segment marine worm larva, nerves and non-nerves alike. The wiring shows how sensors can reach cilia, glands, pigment, and muscle throughout the body.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes of a species are often architecturally similar, implying that connectivity is genetically encoded in part. A model that links gene expression to wiring could generate testable circuit motifs.
ocar.challenge: Where and how neuronal connectivity is encoded, and what graph signature genetically driven synapse and gap-junction rules would leave, was not formalized.
ocar.action: Barabási and Barabási hypothesize that genetic identity guides synapse and gap-junction formation, predict biclique motifs, and search for large, statistically significant bicliques in connectomes of three species, comparing them with expression and morphology.
ocar.resolution: They find significant maximal bicliques in C. elegans chemical and gap-junction maps (similar significance diagrams across reconstructions), in Ciona intestinalis CNS (N = 205 neurons, L = 2,974 edges), and in the Drosophila larva olfactory circuit (N = 387, L = 3,690). Many C. elegans biclique neurons share expression patterns despite coverage of only 935 of about 20,000 genes. The same framework is proposed for neuromodulatory 'wireless' bicliques.
ocar.future_work: Definitive tests need fuller connectomes with matched expression. Whether the model formalizes mammalian circuit development is posed as an open question.

summaries.beginner: If genes tell neurons whom to connect to, the wiring diagram should contain a telltale pattern: two groups of cells in which everyone on one side talks to everyone on the other. This paper finds those patterns in worm, sea squirt, and fly-larva maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2020), D. L. Barabási and A.-L. Barabási treat genetically guided synaptogenesis as operators that imprint maximal bicliques on the connectome. They report statistically significant bicliques in multiple C. elegans maps, Ciona CNS, and a Drosophila larval olfactory circuit, with shared expression inside many worm bicliques. The model yields falsifiable predictions about genes driving specific circuits and extends, in principle, to extrasynaptic modulator systems.
summaries.advanced: Bicliques are statistical graph features, not proven molecular mechanisms for each motif. C. elegans expression covers 935 genes. Ciona and fly analyses demonstrate bicliques but lack the same expression test in the selected extract. A.-L. Barabási's company roles are declared. Mammalian generalization is speculative. Local experience-dependent variation is acknowledged as outside a purely genetic imprint.

plain_language_summary: If genes tell neurons whom to connect to, the wiring diagram should contain a telltale pattern: two groups of cells in which everyone on one side talks to everyone on the other. This paper finds those patterns in worm, sea squirt, and fly-larva maps.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM remains the gold standard for synapses and morphology, but speed has limited mammalian volumes. A parallel, autonomous TEM pipeline could reach cortical-microcircuit scale.
ocar.challenge: Imaging a cubic millimeter or more at synaptic resolution requires 24/7 operation, quality control, and horizontal scaling without sacrificing resolution or becoming prohibitively expensive.
ocar.action: Yin, Brittain, Reid, da Costa, and colleagues built piTEAM: six automated TEMs (autoTEMs) imaging sections from one block in parallel. They acquired more than 1 mm³ of mouse neocortex spanning four visual areas.
ocar.resolution: Over 26,500 ultrathin sections yielded more than 2 petabytes in less than 6 months. Combined burst rate is 3 Gpixel/s and net rate 600 Mpixel/s with six microscopes. Moving from 20 to 50 Mpixel cameras cut 1 mm² montage time from 40 min to 15 min. They argue cubic-millimeter cortical microcircuits are now feasible across regions and species.
ocar.future_work: Simulated 100+ Mpixel sensors project about a further 3× speedup; beam-scanning (Voxa Cricket) could cut stage step-and-settle (>100 ms). They anticipate a single microscope net rate rising from 100 to 500 Mpixel/s, about 100 days per mm³. Compact AMT lens assemblies could avoid 4.6 m columns.

summaries.beginner: Taking electron-microscope pictures of a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex used to be out of reach. This team ran six automated transmission microscopes around the clock and finished that volume in under six months.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2020), Yin, Brittain, Reid, da Costa, and colleagues describe piTEAM, a six-microscope automated TEM pipeline. They imaged more than 1 mm³ of mouse neocortex across four visual areas, more than 26,500 sections and more than 2 petabytes, in less than 6 months, at 3 Gpixel/s burst and 600 Mpixel/s net. Fifty-megapixel cameras reduced 1 mm² montages from 40 to 15 minutes. The architecture is designed to scale by adding cameras or microscopes.
summaries.advanced: This paper is an acquisition pipeline and demonstration volume, not a finished mouse cortical connectome. Net versus burst rates differ because of overhead and quality control. Speed projections for 100+ Mpixel sensors and beam-scanning are simulations or R&D tests, not the production 2 PB run. Sectioning 26,500 sections from one block is itself a failure-mode-rich process only partly detailed in the selected extract.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience now acquires data at a scale that outpaces most biomedical fields. Understanding which modalities are information-rich is necessary to plan analysis and learning algorithms.
ocar.challenge: Electron-microscopy connectomics is singled out as especially hard: machine-learning pipelines demand excessive labelled data while using only a small fraction of raw imagery for training, exposing a gap between artificial and biological intelligence.
ocar.action: Motta, Schurr, Staffler, and Helmstaedter review big-data issues in nanoscale connectomics and the field's appetite for training labels.
ocar.resolution: They argue that substantial improvements in label and energy efficiency of machine learning may be required before a nanoscale human-brain connectome is a realistic goal.
ocar.future_work: The review frames efficiency of learning from EM as a prerequisite for human-scale connectomics rather than presenting a new reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope datasets are enormous, yet the computers that trace them still need people to label lots of examples. This review says that mismatch is a central obstacle on the way to a human connectome.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Motta, Schurr, Staffler, and Helmstaedter review why EM connectomics is a particularly hard big-data problem. They emphasize that current machine-learning practice consumes large amounts of labelled data while training on only a small fraction of available imagery. They conclude that better label and energy efficiency may be required to contemplate a nanoscale human brain connectome.
summaries.advanced: This card follows the published abstract: the bundled PDF extract is a different paper (Jiang et al. 2025, mitochondria mapping in webKnossos) and was not used. As a review, it does not report a new volume or a single numeric labelling budget in the abstract. Human-brain feasibility is a forward-looking claim, not a demonstration.

ocar.opportunity: Large connectomes are becoming available and should constrain and test theoretical models of neural computation. Wiring diagrams can in principle turn unconstrained network models into biologically grounded ones.
ocar.challenge: Theoretical neuroscience does not yet have a standard toolkit for inserting connectivity constraints from these datasets into the models it typically studies.
ocar.action: Litwin-Kumar and Turaga survey recent approaches to building models with constrained EM wiring diagrams and the insights those models have provided.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes existing strategies for using connectomes in computation models and argues that new techniques will be needed as datasets grow more complex.
ocar.future_work: Scaling current constraint methods to ever larger and richer reconstructions is presented as an open technical need.

summaries.beginner: Having a wiring diagram is not the same as having a working theory of what the circuit computes. This review asks how to put electron-microscope connection maps into the models theorists already use.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Litwin-Kumar and Turaga survey methods for constraining computational models with EM wiring diagrams. They note that standard tools for this fusion are still lacking, review insights from early constrained models, and call for new techniques as connectomes grow.
summaries.advanced: This card follows the published abstract: the bundled PDF extract is a different paper (Kim et al. 2025, divergent PN-to-LHN synaptic dynamics in Current Biology) and was not used. As a survey, it does not introduce a new algorithm or dataset in the abstract. 'Standard tools' being absent is the authors' assessment as of 2019.
